name: SiteSentinel
title: Always-on safety cameras for a construction site
summary: Watches construction-site CCTV with YOLOv8 models for fire and smoke, workers without hard hats, falls and people in restricted areas, logs each incident with a snapshot and emails the team.

metrics.label: detection models: fire/smoke, helmet, fall, restricted area
cameras at once by default, each with its own worker
growth signals scored to decide whether a fire is spreading
cooldowns before an ongoing incident is logged / emailed again

problem: Site managers can't watch every feed all day, and the hazards that matter most (fire, missing hard hats, falls) become serious in seconds.
Detectors trained on clean photos also struggle with real CCTV, where workers are far away and their heads are only a few pixels tall.

constraints.label: Unattended cameras
constraints.text: Each camera keeps analysing and logging even when nobody has the dashboard open, and reconnects by itself when a stream drops.

constraints.label: Distant workers
constraints.text: On 1080p CCTV heads are small, so the helmet model runs at up to 960 px instead of 640, and small images are never upscaled.

constraints.label: Hardware
constraints.text: Inference uses the NVIDIA GPU when PyTorch can see one and falls back to the CPU otherwise.

constraints.label: Alert fatigue
constraints.text: A violation that lasts for minutes must not flood the incident log or the team's inbox.

architecture.caption: Every camera runs its own background worker that keeps only the newest frame, runs one of four YOLO models on a shared inference thread, logs incidents and serves an annotated MJPEG stream.

sections.heading: Keeping live video live while the model lags behind
paras: Inference is slower than a camera's frame rate, so a plain read loop falls further behind every second. Each camera is wrapped in a reader thread that keeps only the newest frame; the analysis worker waits for a frame newer than the last one it processed, capped at 5 analyses per second.

The same worker handles failure. After about 5 seconds of missed reads the camera is marked gone, the stream shows a 'Reconnecting…' placeholder and the worker retries every 10 seconds. A detection error sets an error state without killing the camera thread.

sections.heading: Deciding when a fire is spreading, not just present
paras: Responders need to know whether a fire is growing. A spread detector keeps a 10-frame history of fire area, velocity and coverage of a 6×6 grid on top of the fire model's boxes.

Eight signals (growth over 2, 3 and 4 frames, short and medium-term trends, velocity, acceleration, new grid cells, region growth) add to a score. Fires below 0.3% of the frame are ignored; 35 or more out of 100 marks the fire as spreading on the stream.

challenges.title: Inference on request threads leaked OS threads
challenges.text: PyTorch creates a native worker pool for every thread that runs a model and never frees it, so inference on Flask's per-request threads leaked about 7 threads per request. All YOLO inference now goes through one single-worker executor.

challenges.title: One head reported as both 'hat' and 'person'
challenges.text: The helmet model could output overlapping helmet and bare-head boxes for one head. Detection now uses class-agnostic NMS, and the raw classes go through a label mapping so only bare heads count as violations.

challenges.title: Ongoing violations flooding the log and inbox
challenges.text: A new kind of violation is logged within 5 seconds, but the same one again only every 30 s. Email has its own 5-minute cooldown per violation and camera and counts what it suppressed.

outcome: SiteSentinel runs several RTSP, HTTP or USB cameras at once, each assigned a model, and streams annotated video to a React dashboard. Uploaded images and videos can be analysed too.
Incidents are stored through SQLAlchemy (SQLite, MySQL or PostgreSQL) with snapshots, exported to CSV and emailed over SMTP. A health page reports device, CPU, memory and per-model latency.
